q2.answer: In the bone of the gum (upper jaw) next to the front teeth. It is called the alveolar cleft.

q3.answer: The small tooth next to the front tooth on the left (lateral incisor) never grew (agenesis). About half of children with a cleft do not have it on the cleft side.

q4.answer: The graft gives the eye tooth bone to come down into. Without bone it has nothing to grow into. The graft also joins the jaw parts, supports the teeth next to the gap and the side of the nose, and closes any hole between mouth and nose.
q4.where: Sheet 1, 'The eye tooth' and 'Why surgeons do the bone graft'

q5.answer: About 8 to 11 years old, but timing depends on how far the teeth have grown, ideally before the eye tooth comes through.

q7.answer: New bone fills the gap and the gum has healed over it. The graft joins the two parts of the upper jaw. The eye tooth is still in the bone but a little lower.
q7.where: Sheet 2, key message box and 'What has changed'

q8.answer: With an X-ray at about 3 to 6 months after surgery, which shows how well the new bone has taken.

q9.answer: The hip can be sore for a while. In one study children went back to school after about 2 weeks.

q10.answer: It has come down through the new bone and is fully in the row of teeth.

q11.answer: Fixed braces. Almost everyone who has this graft needs them.
q11.where: Sheet 3, key message box and 'What has changed'

q12.answer: Two plans. Close the space: braces move the eye tooth into the missing tooth's place, then it is reshaped and filled with tooth-coloured filling (most common for cleft children). Keep the space: a removable plate with a false tooth while still growing, then when growth stops an implant (post with crown) or a bridge (false tooth with one wing glued behind the next tooth). The cleft team discusses which suits you.
